Blood Spatter in the Oscar Pistorius Trial

By: Eugene Botha | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
we look at forensic evidence not raised in the Oscar Pistorius trial

Summary:
Contrary to expectations a remarkable amount of crucial forensic evidence did not surface in the Oscar Pistorius Trial. Evidence about ballistics were not complete and crucial evidence about blood spatter was strangely not raised by either the State or the Defence. In fact, the defence did not call their expert witness on blood splatter at all.

Further information:
Contrary to expectations a remarkable amount of crucial forensic evidence did not surface in the Oscar Pistorius Trial. Evidence about ballistics were not complete and crucial evidence about blood spatter was strangely not raised by either the State or the Defence. In fact, the defence did not call their expert witness on blood splatter at all.

There was one glaring omission in the evidence on blood. The toilet. The toilet not only held a bullet fragment that the police missed completely and which was found by the defence experts, but the blood stain pattern in the toilet was never raised by either party. And yet, it is crucial evidence because photographs of the toilet would suggest that it had been flushed seconds before the shooting occurred. This has all kinds of ramifications.

We have asked forensic experts Wollie Wolmarans and Cobus Steyl to take a look at the blood spatter evidence and the crime scene with fresh eyes and give their interpretation.

They will not only look at the toilet and the toilet bowl, but at all the blood spatter throughout the house and investigate if it corresponds with the evidence led at the trial. We have access to Inspector Ian van der Nest's report on the blood spatter and we have crime scene photographs of the whole scene.

Different kinds of blood splatter were found on the scene such as low, medium and high velocity, high velocity patterns, drip, transfer, impact and cast-off stains. Looking at these aspects a trained analyst can conclude an awful amount about what happened and if the blood tells the same story as the accused.

We will use real blood to explain the various kinds of blood stain patterns that were found on the scene, and we will also recreate the toilet bowl scenario and ask why this crucial evidence was missed by both the defence and the prosecution.

AMALIA
• Duration... too long... cut it down and lets
• Not clear why we are doing this at first and for too long
• Bring sense of intrigue forward must arrive earlier
• Did we say vd Nest was state blood spatter expert
• Add in Pretoria to the address on screen in the beginning...
• Just to go from bottom to bathroom too abrupt
• Indicate it’s a doll in the pics the first time we see it.
• Take too long to tell us that we are seeing van der nest
• Subtitles translatons
• Aerials show his house
• Please put into new script that the water timing showed it runs for 11 seconds after flushing
• Send script and questions to Dario and they will send rights of reply off.
• It has been sent to George
DARIO
1. **We must warn about images not for children, sensitive viewers – it needs a 16 throughout the story
2. Derek says in a link it would have made a huge difference to the trial – it could possibly have made a difference rather put into voice over.
3. would like the script to make some changes
4. this seems based on Barry’s book
5. Footage of the re-enactment ? Eugene: it was given to me by Wollie Wolmarans who witnessed it, they are his photos.
6. What does Wollie say bout the toilet issue? E: that he only noticed it after he testified and admits he over looked it. He agrees toilet was flushed and says vd Nest did a good job. Wollie was there to look at ballistics
7. Did vd nest not notice it?
8. Are we 100% sure account that says toilet was flushed before she died is correct? Eugene. It can only have happened this way. It was not flushed after the wood and blood was deposited there. Wollie and Cobus both concur that it was flushed before and we timed water running on inside of the bowl. Also, Wes vd Westhuizen was state blood spatter expert but they didn’t call him as he had questionable credentials.
9. Where we say in the script that a time line was raised in the trial but that the judge ultimately accepted the timeline presented by the defence – say this.
10. Change: new evidence has resulted in a number of people questions raised around the timeline – who are they? E: Cobus referred to it by Barry, off the record Wollie, and other forensic guys like Reggie Perumal. Because the photos had not been made available to the public before the trial.
11. At the simulation with stained liquid... don’t say Cobus is spot on... the endorsement of his conclusion isn’t ideal
12. Was uncomfortable with Barry saying raises q around OP version but you do balance it with saying this could have helped state and defence. But there are some of Barry’s other statements we need to remove audience must not be left thinking OP is lying and he got off. Take out Barry saying suggestion is there it was purposely overlooked and didn’t fit their narrative. And leave Llewelyn’s comment in that it was overlooked.
13. Do we need to go to state and defence for reply? If we are criticising them we should – Dario says they can do a covering letter with Eugene’s questions attached – we are doing a story on this and there is a question about were you aware and if so why was this not presented to the court? And we send this to both sides.
14. We need to get Ian Van Der Nests’ right of reply? We should ask Van Der Nest. E: there was nothing about this in his report submitted to court...
15. Wes vd Westhuizen didn’t testify so we dont need to go to him.
16. The CPA Section 123 says you cannot publish an account of a crime that deviates from a court record except with permission from the commissioner of correctional services. This is there to protect prisoners’ dignity post trial and sentencing... Its a risk-management exercise and we can balance this with public interest – but this is what Brian Webber can use to get an interdict.. unlikely to get permission and it will take forever so I wouldn’t ask. And we take the risk that webber doesn’t know about sec 123.

Press Release:


Oscar Trial: evidence overlooked?
During the Oscar Pistorius trial, forensic blood stain pattern analysis of the crime scene was found to support Oscar’s version of events after the shooting. Yet, no blood stain pattern analysis relevant to events before the shooting was presented to the court. Now, re-analysis of pictures of the crime scene made public during the trial have led to the suggestion that curious patterns observed in the blood in the toilet bowl could mean that the toilet was flushed seconds before Reeva was shot. Carte Blanche asks: could both the prosecution and defence perhaps have overlooked crucial evidence?


Script:


LINK:
On Valentine’s Day 2013 this house was the centre of world attention. News broke that in the early hours of that morning Olympic athlete Oscar Pistorius shot 4 times through a locked toilet door and killed his model girlfriend, Reeva Steenkamp.
V/O:
This is what the house looks like today. It has been repainted on the inside but the house is still unoccupied. There is an upper story accessed via a staircase. Upstairs there are 3 bedrooms, including a master bedroom. The bathroom in which Reeva was shot is reached through a short passage leading from the master bedroom. The house has since been cleaned and all traces of the crime removed. But on that fateful day a very different scene unfolded here.
LINK:
There was blood spatter all over the house, and the trail started here in the toilet adjacent in the main bathroom. There was a pool of blood in the cubicle and a pool of blood just here, outside the cubicle.
V/O:
In forensic science blood stain patterns can tell a scientifically accurate story about the events that took place on a crime scene. And in the Pistorius case the blood evidence sheds light on two crucial timelines – what happened before the shooting and what took place afterwards.

Curiously, only blood spatter evidence relating to the timeline of what happened after the shooting was brought before court. However, also visible in the blood stains were significant clues as to what had happened before the shooting. This evidence was never presented.

A few days after Reeva’s death police blood spatter expert Col Ian van der Nest used a mannequin to re-enact the timeline of what happened after the shooting. He based this on blood spatter found on the scene.

This photograph shows the position in which Oscar Pistorius found Reeva.

The following photographs show how he removed her from the toilet cubicle and put her down on the bathroom floor.

That night there was also a bloodstained cricket bat, pistol and cell phone on the bathroom floor.

He then picked her up again and carried her from the bathroom and through the bedroom and a small TV room.

This left a trail of blood – on the walls, on a case containing watches, on the tiles and on the railing bordering the top floor.
LINK:
The blood trail then came down these stairs. There was extensive blood spatter on this wall and on the furniture in the lounge below.
V/O:
She was put down at the bottom of the stairs. Colonel van der Nest testified during the trial.
Gerrie Nel:
What was your interest at the crime scene?

Van der Nest:
M'Lady, my interest was there to address several investigative questions which were posed to me. These included the appearance of blunt force trauma on the deceased’s body… the extensive staining at the scene as well as the blood stained cricket bat. I was asked to give an opinion as whether blunt force trauma, was that responsible for some or all of the splatter that was visualised throughout the house.
V/O:
To help us evaluate his testimony we turned to two private forensic experts: Cobus Steyl, a ballistics and blood spatter expert and Wollie Wolmarans, also a ballistics expert. Wollie witnessed van der Nests re-enactment a few days after the shooting and also acted as expert ballistics witness for the defence. Both agree that blood spatter analysis can be crucial to a forensic investigation.
Wollie:
Blood spatter basically tells a story, also to the forensic expert. He can then tell where certain actions took place, for example was someone hit at a point in time? Was a shot fired? And it can tell you that something happened here that needs to be looked into.
V/O:
The shape and size of the droplets can reveal whether blood stains were caused by a victim having been hit with an object or shot. The patterns created in this way are known as active blood stain patterns.

But there are also passive stains. These include dripping, flows and pools of blood.

Transfer stains result from objects coming into contact with existing bloodstains and leaving wipes, swipes or pattern transfers behind such as a bloody shoe print or a smear.

And other sorts of patterns reveal whether or not a person was still alive when the blood event occurred.
Cobus:
And then quite important, you get your arterial spurts. It is when one of your arteries has been severed or breached and that can create, due to the blood pressure, little spurts. It can also give you a tell-tale sign that is an arterial spurt, the volume of blood and the direction. What they call the S-type, a zig-zag from that you can observe.
V/O:
Based on established principles of blood spatter analysis such as these, Colonel van der Nest concluded that the extensive blood spatter patterns all over the Pistorius house were mainly passive patterns, and that they were caused by dripping blood or cast-off blood flung from Reeva’s blood soaked hair.

A few arterial spurts were also observed indicating that she was still alive when Pistorius carried her.

Van der Nest concluded that the blood on the bat was also caused by Reeva’s dripping blood, and that she was not hit with it.
LINK:
And early on the morning of the 14th of February, pictures of Oscar Pistorius were taken here, in the garage wearing his prosthetic legs.
V/O:
The right hand side of his shorts was soaked in blood. Van der Nest concluded that this, as well as the other blood spatter evidence on the scene, fully supported Pistorius’ version of events after the shooting.

Both Cobus and Wollie have high regard for van der Nest’s work, and agree with this interpretation.
Wollie:
It was absolutely objective and correctly done in my opinion. And I can say the little I knew at that stage about the background and the statements made by Oscar, fully agreed with the version that he gave from the beginning.
LINK:
So the testimony of van der Nest confirmed Pistorius’ timeline of events after the shooting of how he had found her and carried her down these stairs to the bottom. This timeline was not questioned.
V/O:
The other timeline raised during the trial was the timeline of what had happened before Reeva was shot.

Barry Bateman is an EWN journalist who followed the case closely and co-authored a best-selling book on it all. He says the state and defence each had their own version of this crucial timeline.
Barry Bateman:
What the State was arguing was that there was this fight, Reeva Steenkamp fled to the bathroom in fear. Oscar Pistorius in a fit of rage fetched his firearm, followed her down there. And it came to these moments in the bathroom, this crucial seconds where the State says Reeva was standing behind the door, Oscar Pistorius was on the other side shouting and screaming, he was angry and he opened fire.

There was also the other side where Oscar Pistorius says he was in fear, coming down into the bathroom, he didn’t know who was behind the door, thinking it was an intruder, he was vulnerable because he was on his stumps, and having his firearm pointed towards the door, he heard the noise behind it there and that was the reaction he had and opened fire four times.
V/O:
So the State and defence disagreed on the timeline of what had happened just before the shooting. In the end, Judge Masipa accepted Pistorius’ version of events as being consistent with the objective evidence.

But, as more photographs of the crime scene became public during the trial, suggestions were put forward that there was indeed possible blood spatter evidence that could shed light on the crucial seconds before Reeva was shot.
LINK:
And this evidence entailed curious blood patterns observed in photos taken of this toilet bowl around six in the morning after the shooting.
Barry B:
If you go have a look at the crime scene photographs and specifically those photos that were taken inside that toilet cubicle and you look down into the toilet bowl you will see it looks like a candy cane. It is the bowl that is smeared with the red of the blood which is separated by columns of white where you see the porcelain
V/O:
At the time Barry asked Cobus Steyl to examine photographs of the toilet bowl.
Cobus:
What is interesting to note in the toilet is that we have here a pattern of blood which is like your stain pattern inside the bowl section but very peculiar you have these clean portions in this section which gives you an indication that blood has been rubbed away or wiped away.
V/O:
These observations saw Cobus conclude that Reeva was shot, fell down and bled into the toilet bowl seconds after she had flushed it. The residual dripping of water after the flush washed the clean lines into the blood.

We simulated the event in the actual toilet, using stained dishwashing liquid. The toilet continues to drip in various places for about 18 seconds after it is flushed, and this could have created the patterns in the blood.

The toilet could not have been flushed accidentally and the patterns observed also suggest that the toilet was not flushed after Reeva fell and bled into it.
Cobus:
The toilet was not flushed here because you can see here in the bottom section there is still blood and you can see wood, in fact if you zoom in, there are wood portions sticking to the surface in the blood. So there was no water that created a flush or a gush after this blood was being created.
V/O:
Close-up photographs also reveal that the toilet was not leaking on that day. Cobus is of the opinion that the clean lines in the blood in the toilet bowl could only have been created in the seconds after Reeva was shot while there was still some water dripping.
Barry B:
It was a startling piece of evidence that had not come out in the trial. But what is does it is potentially changing to the State’s case and the defence’s case had it been presented. It raises then raises questions about Oscar’s version who says he was screaming and shouting at the burglar to get out of my house.
V/O:
But the possible flushing of the toilet also undermines the state’s case against Pistorius.
Barry B:
The State was saying there was an argument, there was a fight, and in a fit of rage he opened fire. It confirms his version, Oscar’s version that his girlfriend he went to the toilet to relieve herself.
V/O:
So the fact that the toilet may have been flushed before Reeva was shot, could have assisted both the prosecution and the defence, but it was never put before court. The question is why?
Barry:
It did not fit their narrative. But ultimately how much of a role would it have played? It should have been put before the judge to decide.
V/O:
But it wasn’t. Dr. Llewelyn Curlewis is a Pretoria attorney who followed the Pistorius trial closely as a commentator for SkyNews.
Llewelyn:
From an ethical pint of view one would have expected both counsel, when there is something relevant that can assist the court to get to a just conclusion they must advance that evidence to court and they must produce it before court.
Derek:
So can we assume that neither party, Prosecution or Defence knew about the toilet issue?
Llewelyn:
One can safely assume that is the only reasonable conclusion under the circumstances, otherwise why did they not disclose it to court?
V/O:
So, did the two sides know about the flushing of the toilet? We asked them.

Both the South African Police Service and the prosecution concurred that they could not comment “…due to an upcoming appeal process in this case”.

Brain Webber, Oscar Pistorius’s attorney replied to us:
‘There was no evidence at the trial or any credible and acceptable evidence (photographic or otherwise) available at the time that “the toilet had been flushed shortly before Reeva Steenkamp was shot.” Such version is contrary to both the State’s version and the defence version.’
V/O:
So it seems that the possibility that the toilet was flushed before the shooting may have been completely overlooked by both prosecution and defence experts who examined the crime scene.

But if this is new evidence, can it be used to re-open the case?
Llewelyn:
Our Criminal Procedure Act in terms of Section 316 determine that you can apply to court to introduce new evidence. In that instance it is a new application, the court must be convinced that the new evidence might have a different outcome of the case altogether. You must also plead under oath why you did not introduce it in the first instance. It can certainly have an influence on the outcome of the case and it is still something they can consider. However in this instance it hasn’t happened up to now and I cannot see that it will happen before it is attend to in the Supreme Court of Appeal.
LINK:
The Appeal is set be heard in November of this year, but the question remains: how much different would the outcome of the case have been if either the police or defence had noticed the peculiar stains in this toilet bowl right from the start?
Barry:
It will be one of those lingering questions that we will be left with in the trail of Oscar Pistorius.

During the Oscar Pistorius trial, forensic blood stain pattern analysis of the crime scene was found to support Oscar’s version of events after the shooting. Yet, no blood stain pattern analysis relevant to events before the shooting was presented to the court. Now, re-analysis of pictures of the crime scene made public during the trial have led to the suggestion that curious patterns observed in the blood in the toilet bowl could mean that the toilet was flushed seconds before Reeva was shot. Carte Blanche asks: could both the prosecution and defence perhaps have overlooked crucial evidence? Script: LINK: On Valentine’s Day 2013 this house was the centre of world attention. News broke that in the early hours of that morning Olympic athlete Oscar Pistorius shot 4 times through a locked toilet door and killed his model girlfriend, Reeva Steenkamp. V/O: This is what the house looks like today. It has been repainted on the inside but the house is still unoccupied. There is an upper story accessed via a staircase. Upstairs there are 3 bedrooms, including a master bedroom. The bathroom in which Reeva was shot is reached through a short passage leading from the master bedroom. The house has since been cleaned and all traces of the crime removed. But on that fateful day a very different scene unfolded here. LINK: There was blood spatter all over the house, and the trail started here in the toilet adjacent in the main bathroom. There was a pool of blood in the cubicle and a pool of blood just here, outside the cubicle. V/O: In forensic science blood stain patterns can tell a scientifically accurate story about the events that took place on a crime scene. And in the Pistorius case the blood evidence sheds light on two crucial timelines – what happened before the shooting and what took place afterwards. Curiously, only blood spatter evidence relating to the timeline of what happened after the shooting was brought before court. However, also visible in the blood stains were significant clues as to what had happened before the shooting. This evidence was never presented. A few days after Reeva’s death police blood spatter expert Col Ian van der Nest used a mannequin to re-enact the timeline of what happened after the shooting. He based this on blood spatter found on the scene. This photograph shows the position in which Oscar Pistorius found Reeva. The following photographs show how he removed her from the toilet cubicle and put her down on the bathroom floor. That night there was also a bloodstained cricket bat, pistol and cell phone on the bathroom floor. He then picked her up again and carried her from the bathroom and through the bedroom and a small TV room. This left a trail of blood – on the walls, on a case containing watches, on the tiles and on the railing bordering the top floor. LINK: The blood trail then came down these stairs. There was extensive blood spatter on this wall and on the furniture in the lounge below. V/O: She was put down at the bottom of the stairs. Colonel van der Nest testified during the trial. Gerrie Nel: What was your interest at the crime scene? Van der Nest: M'Lady, my interest was there to address several investigative questions which were posed to me. These included the appearance of blunt force trauma on the deceased’s body… the extensive staining at the scene as well as the blood stained cricket bat. I was asked to give an opinion as whether blunt force trauma, was that responsible for some or all of the splatter that was visualised throughout the house. V/O: To help us evaluate his testimony we turned to two private forensic experts: Cobus Steyl, a ballistics and blood spatter expert and Wollie Wolmarans, also a ballistics expert. Wollie witnessed van der Nests re-enactment a few days after the shooting and also acted as expert ballistics witness for the defence. Both agree that blood spatter analysis can be crucial to a forensic investigation. Wollie: Blood spatter basically tells a story, also to the forensic expert. He can then tell where certain actions took place, for example was someone hit at a point in time? Was a shot fired? And it can tell you that something happened here that needs to be looked into. V/O: The shape and size of the droplets can reveal whether blood stains were caused by a victim having been hit with an object or shot. The patterns created in this way are known as active blood stain patterns. But there are also passive stains. These include dripping, flows and pools of blood. Transfer stains result from objects coming into contact with existing bloodstains and leaving wipes, swipes or pattern transfers behind such as a bloody shoe print or a smear. And other sorts of patterns reveal whether or not a person was still alive when the blood event occurred. Cobus: And then quite important, you get your arterial spurts. It is when one of your arteries has been severed or breached and that can create, due to the blood pressure, little spurts. It can also give you a tell-tale sign that is an arterial spurt, the volume of blood and the direction. What they call the S-type, a zig-zag from that you can observe. V/O: Based on established principles of blood spatter analysis such as these, Colonel van der Nest concluded that the extensive blood spatter patterns all over the Pistorius house were mainly passive patterns, and that they were caused by dripping blood or cast-off blood flung from Reeva’s blood soaked hair. A few arterial spurts were also observed indicating that she was still alive when Pistorius carried her. Van der Nest concluded that the blood on the bat was also caused by Reeva’s dripping blood, and that she was not hit with it. LINK: And early on the morning of the 14th of February, pictures of Oscar Pistorius were taken here, in the garage wearing his prosthetic legs. V/O: The right hand side of his shorts was soaked in blood. Van der Nest concluded that this, as well as the other blood spatter evidence on the scene, fully supported Pistorius’ version of events after the shooting. Both Cobus and Wollie have high regard for van der Nest’s work, and agree with this interpretation. Wollie: It was absolutely objective and correctly done in my opinion. And I can say the little I knew at that stage about the background and the statements made by Oscar, fully agreed with the version that he gave from the beginning. LINK: So the testimony of van der Nest confirmed Pistorius’ timeline of events after the shooting of how he had found her and carried her down these stairs to the bottom. This timeline was not questioned. V/O: The other timeline raised during the trial was the timeline of what had happened before Reeva was shot. Barry Bateman is an EWN journalist who followed the case closely and co-authored a best-selling book on it all. He says the state and defence each had their own version of this crucial timeline. Barry Bateman: What the State was arguing was that there was this fight, Reeva Steenkamp fled to the bathroom in fear. Oscar Pistorius in a fit of rage fetched his firearm, followed her down there. And it came to these moments in the bathroom, this crucial seconds where the State says Reeva was standing behind the door, Oscar Pistorius was on the other side shouting and screaming, he was angry and he opened fire. There was also the other side where Oscar Pistorius says he was in fear, coming down into the bathroom, he didn’t know who was behind the door, thinking it was an intruder, he was vulnerable because he was on his stumps, and having his firearm pointed towards the door, he heard the noise behind it there and that was the reaction he had and opened fire four times. V/O: So the State and defence disagreed on the timeline of what had happened just before the shooting. In the end, Judge Masipa accepted Pistorius’ version of events as being consistent with the objective evidence. But, as more photographs of the crime scene became public during the trial, suggestions were put forward that there was indeed possible blood spatter evidence that could shed light on the crucial seconds before Reeva was shot. LINK: And this evidence entailed curious blood patterns observed in photos taken of this toilet bowl around six in the morning after the shooting. Barry B: If you go have a look at the crime scene photographs and specifically those photos that were taken inside that toilet cubicle and you look down into the toilet bowl you will see it looks like a candy cane. It is the bowl that is smeared with the red of the blood which is separated by columns of white where you see the porcelain V/O: At the time Barry asked Cobus Steyl to examine photographs of the toilet bowl. Cobus: What is interesting to note in the toilet is that we have here a pattern of blood which is like your stain pattern inside the bowl section but very peculiar you have these clean portions in this section which gives you an indication that blood has been rubbed away or wiped away. V/O: These observations saw Cobus conclude that Reeva was shot, fell down and bled into the toilet bowl seconds after she had flushed it. The residual dripping of water after the flush washed the clean lines into the blood. We simulated the event in the actual toilet, using stained dishwashing liquid. The toilet continues to drip in various places for about 18 seconds after it is flushed, and this could have created the patterns in the blood. The toilet could not have been flushed accidentally and the patterns observed also suggest that the toilet was not flushed after Reeva fell and bled into it. Cobus: The toilet was not flushed here because you can see here in the bottom section there is still blood and you can see wood, in fact if you zoom in, there are wood portions sticking to the surface in the blood. So there was no water that created a flush or a gush after this blood was being created. V/O: Close-up photographs also reveal that the toilet was not leaking on that day. Cobus is of the opinion that the clean lines in the blood in the toilet bowl could only have been created in the seconds after Reeva was shot while there was still some water dripping. Barry B: It was a startling piece of evidence that had not come out in the trial. But what is does it is potentially changing to the State’s case and the defence’s case had it been presented. It raises then raises questions about Oscar’s version who says he was screaming and shouting at the burglar to get out of my house. V/O: But the possible flushing of the toilet also undermines the state’s case against Pistorius. Barry B: The State was saying there was an argument, there was a fight, and in a fit of rage he opened fire. It confirms his version, Oscar’s version that his girlfriend he went to the toilet to relieve herself. V/O: So the fact that the toilet may have been flushed before Reeva was shot, could have assisted both the prosecution and the defence, but it was never put before court. The question is why? Barry: It did not fit their narrative. But ultimately how much of a role would it have played? It should have been put before the judge to decide. V/O: But it wasn’t. Dr. Llewelyn Curlewis is a Pretoria attorney who followed the Pistorius trial closely as a commentator for SkyNews. Llewelyn: From an ethical pint of view one would have expected both counsel, when there is something relevant that can assist the court to get to a just conclusion they must advance that evidence to court and they must produce it before court. Derek: So can we assume that neither party, Prosecution or Defence knew about the toilet issue? Llewelyn: One can safely assume that is the only reasonable conclusion under the circumstances, otherwise why did they not disclose it to court? V/O: So, did the two sides know about the flushing of the toilet? We asked them. Both the South African Police Service and the prosecution concurred that they could not comment “…due to an upcoming appeal process in this case”. Brain Webber, Oscar Pistorius’s attorney replied to us: ‘There was no evidence at the trial or any credible and acceptable evidence (photographic or otherwise) available at the time that “the toilet had been flushed shortly before Reeva Steenkamp was shot.” Such version is contrary to both the State’s version and the defence version.’ V/O: So it seems that the possibility that the toilet was flushed before the shooting may have been completely overlooked by both prosecution and defence experts who examined the crime scene. But if this is new evidence, can it be used to re-open the case? Llewelyn: Our Criminal Procedure Act in terms of Section 316 determine that you can apply to court to introduce new evidence. In that instance it is a new application, the court must be convinced that the new evidence might have a different outcome of the case altogether. You must also plead under oath why you did not introduce it in the first instance. It can certainly have an influence on the outcome of the case and it is still something they can consider. However in this instance it hasn’t happened up to now and I cannot see that it will happen before it is attend to in the Supreme Court of Appeal. LINK: The Appeal is set be heard in November of this year, but the question remains: how much different would the outcome of the case have been if either the police or defence had noticed the peculiar stains in this toilet bowl right from the start? Barry: It will be one of those lingering questions that we will be left with in the trail of Oscar Pistorius. metadata.Summary: Contrary to expectations a remarkable amount of crucial forensic evidence did not surface in the Oscar Pistorius Trial. Evidence about ballistics were not complete and crucial evidence about blood spatter was strangely not raised by either the State or the Defence. In fact, the defence did not call their expert witness on blood splatter at all.
metadata.Further information: Contrary to expectations a remarkable amount of crucial forensic evidence did not surface in the Oscar Pistorius Trial. Evidence about ballistics were not complete and crucial evidence about blood spatter was strangely not raised by either the State or the Defence. In fact, the defence did not call their expert witness on blood splatter at all. There was one glaring omission in the evidence on blood. The toilet. The toilet not only held a bullet fragment that the police missed completely and which was found by the defence experts, but the blood stain pattern in the toilet was never raised by either party. And yet, it is crucial evidence because photographs of the toilet would suggest that it had been flushed seconds before the shooting occurred. This has all kinds of ramifications. We have asked forensic experts Wollie Wolmarans and Cobus Steyl to take a look at the blood spatter evidence and the crime scene with fresh eyes and give their interpretation. They will not only look at the toilet and the toilet bowl, but at all the blood spatter throughout the house and investigate if it corresponds with the evidence led at the trial. We have access to Inspector Ian van der Nest's report on the blood spatter and we have crime scene photographs of the whole scene. Different kinds of blood splatter were found on the scene such as low, medium and high velocity, high velocity patterns, drip, transfer, impact and cast-off stains. Looking at these aspects a trained analyst can conclude an awful amount about what happened and if the blood tells the same story as the accused. We will use real blood to explain the various kinds of blood stain patterns that were found on the scene, and we will also recreate the toilet bowl scenario and ask why this crucial evidence was missed by both the defence and the prosecution.

Derek says in a link it would have made a huge difference to the trial – it could possibly have made a difference rather put into voice over. 3. would like the script to make some changes 4. this seems based on Barry’s book 5. Footage of the re-enactment ? Eugene: it was given to me by Wollie Wolmarans who witnessed it, they are his photos. 6. What does Wollie say bout the toilet issue? E: that he only noticed it after he testified and admits he over looked it. He agrees toilet was flushed and says vd Nest did a good job. Wollie was there to look at ballistics 7. Did vd nest not notice it? 8. Are we 100% sure account that says toilet was flushed before she died is correct? Eugene. It can only have happened this way. It was not flushed after the wood and blood was deposited there. Wollie and Cobus both concur that it was flushed before and we timed water running on inside of the bowl. Also, Wes vd Westhuizen was state blood spatter expert but they didn’t call him as he had questionable credentials. 9. Where we say in the script that a time line was raised in the trial but that the judge ultimately accepted the timeline presented by the defence – say this. 10. Change: new evidence has resulted in a number of people questions raised around the timeline – who are they? E: Cobus referred to it by Barry, off the record Wollie, and other forensic guys like Reggie Perumal. Because the photos had not been made available to the public before the trial. 11. At the simulation with stained liquid... don’t say Cobus is spot on... the endorsement of his conclusion isn’t ideal 12. Was uncomfortable with Barry saying raises q around OP version but you do balance it with saying this could have helped state and defence. But there are some of Barry’s other statements we need to remove audience must not be left thinking OP is lying and he got off. Take out Barry saying suggestion is there it was purposely overlooked and didn’t fit their narrative. And leave Llewelyn’s comment in that it was overlooked. 13. Do we need to go to state and defence for reply? If we are criticising them we should – Dario says they can do a covering letter with Eugene’s questions attached – we are doing a story on this and there is a question about were you aware and if so why was this not presented to the court? And we send this to both sides. 14. We need to get Ian Van Der Nests’ right of reply? We should ask Van Der Nest. E: there was nothing about this in his report submitted to court... 15. Wes vd Westhuizen didn’t testify so we dont need to go to him. 16. The CPA Section 123 says you cannot publish an account of a crime that deviates from a court record except with permission from the commissioner of correctional services. This is there to protect prisoners’ dignity post trial and sentencing... Its a risk-management exercise and we can balance this with public interest – but this is what Brian Webber can use to get an interdict.. unlikely to get permission and it will take forever so I wouldn’t ask. And we take the risk that webber doesn’t know about sec 123.
